gaps.sentence: Library books ___ be taken out of the reading room.
gaps.hint: a passive prohibition with mustn't be
gaps.explanation: Prohibitions can be passive: mustn't be taken.

gaps.sentence: You ___ have seen a ghost — there is no such thing!
gaps.hint: a past claim rejected as impossible
gaps.explanation: 'Can't have' rejects a past claim as impossible: can't have seen.

gaps.sentence: Her car is not in the car park and her office light is off, so she ___ home.
gaps.hint: a confident conclusion about the past
gaps.explanation: A confident conclusion about the past uses 'must have' plus the participle: must have gone.

gaps.sentence: I ___ work late every Wednesday this month; it is a new company policy.
gaps.hint: obligation imposed by an external rule
gaps.explanation: 'Have to' expresses obligation imposed by external rules: have to work.

gaps.hint: a polite offer with would you like
gaps.explanation: 'Would you like' makes a polite offer: Would.

gaps.sentence: You ___ park here — the police tow cars away every morning.
gaps.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a rule you must not break: mustn't park.

gaps.sentence: I ___ have known you were in hospital — nobody told me.
gaps.explanation: 'Couldn't have' means it was impossible to do: couldn't have known.

gaps.sentence: He ___ not have heard the announcement — he had headphones on the whole flight.
gaps.explanation: 'Can't have heard' — 'can' supplies the negative deduction before 'not have heard'.
